title: Collections: List, Set and Map
summary: Store groups of values with ArrayList, keep values unique with HashSet and TreeSet, and map keys to values with HashMap, LinkedHashMap and TreeMap, with every output shown.
introduction: Arrays have a fixed size and no helpful methods; the Java Collections Framework provides resizable, searchable, sortable containers for almost every situation. This lesson introduces the three interfaces you will use daily: List for ordered sequences, Set for unique values and Map for key-value pairs, together with their standard implementations. You add, remove, search, sort and iterate, see which implementation keeps which order, and meet the two mistakes that bite everyone once: removing by index instead of by value, and modifying a list while looping over it.
learningObjectives: Create and modify an ArrayList and iterate over it
Use HashSet and TreeSet to keep values unique, ordered or not
Store and look up key-value pairs with HashMap, LinkedHashMap and TreeMap
Pick the right collection and avoid the common removal mistakes

blocks.text: A `List` keeps elements in insertion order, allows duplicates and gives every element an index. `ArrayList` is the implementation to reach for. The element type goes in angle brackets and must be a class, so a list of whole numbers is `List<Integer>`, never `List<int>`; autoboxing converts the primitives for you. Declare the variable with the interface type `List` and create an `ArrayList`: the code then depends only on the contract, and `new ArrayList<>()` with the empty diamond lets the compiler repeat the element type.

blocks.text: Printing a list shows its elements in square brackets, which is handy for debugging. `getFirst()` and `getLast()` arrived in Java 21 alongside `reversed()`; on older versions use `get(0)` and `get(size() - 1)`.

`List.of(...)` builds an **unmodifiable** list in one expression: perfect for constants and test data, but any attempt to add or remove throws `UnsupportedOperationException`. To get a modifiable copy, pass it to the `ArrayList` constructor. `Collections.sort` orders a list of comparable elements such as numbers or strings in place.

blocks.text: A `Set` holds each value at most once; adding a duplicate is ignored and `add` returns `false` to tell you. `HashSet` is the fastest and makes **no promise about order**: never rely on the order in which it prints. `LinkedHashSet` remembers insertion order, and `TreeSet` keeps its elements sorted. Sets answer the questions *have I seen this before?* and *how many distinct values are there?* in one line.

blocks.text: A `Map` associates each **key** with one **value**: product name to stock level, user id to user, word to count. `put` adds or replaces, `get` returns the value or `null` when the key is absent, and `getOrDefault` avoids that `null`. `merge` combines a new value with an existing one in a single call, which makes counting a one-liner. `HashMap` is unordered, `LinkedHashMap` keeps insertion order and `TreeMap` sorts by key; the example uses `LinkedHashMap` so the output is predictable.

blocks.text: `Integer::sum` is a **method reference**, a compact way to pass the `sum` method as the combining function; the [Records, Enums and Streams](/tutorials/java/records-streams) lesson covers lambdas and method references properly. Iterating `entrySet()` visits key and value together; `keySet()` and `values()` give just one side.

blocks.text: `List` has two `remove` methods: `remove(int index)` and `remove(Object value)`. For a `List<Integer>` the call `numbers.remove(1)` matches the `int` version and removes the element at index 1, not the value 1. Pass `Integer.valueOf(1)` to remove by value. The second trap is removing elements inside an enhanced `for` loop over the same list, which throws `ConcurrentModificationException` on the next iteration. Use `removeIf` with a condition instead.

Do not trust HashMap and HashSet order
blocks.text: `HashMap` and `HashSet` may print their contents in any order, and that order can change when elements are added or when you upgrade Java. Code that passes a test only because the elements happened to come out in insertion order is a bug waiting for production. When order matters, say so with `LinkedHashMap`, `TreeMap` or an explicit sort.

questions.question: Which collection stores values and silently ignores an attempt to add a value it already contains?
questions.explanation: A `Set` holds each value once: `add` returns `false` for a duplicate and the set is unchanged. Lists accept duplicates, and a map stores key-value pairs.

questions.question: A `HashMap` guarantees that its entries are iterated in the order they were inserted.
questions.explanation: `HashMap` makes no ordering promise. `LinkedHashMap` keeps insertion order and `TreeMap` sorts by key.
